title: How To Handle Six Disrespectful Students In One Class -one-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a reader whose class had six chronically disruptive, disrespectful students, Linsin argues that handling multiple difficult students individually — one-on-one talking-tos, behavior contracts, personalized rewards — actually worsens the problem by encouraging resentment and cementing a "difficult" label. He reframes a class with several consistently disrespectful students as a classroom management problem rather than an individual-student problem, requiring the teacher to start over: establish sharply defined, non-negotiable boundaries for all students, teach and model the plan thoroughly, and defend it consistently without pulling anyone aside for scolding or bribery. He describes the expected trajectory — well-behaved students respond first, then difficult students join one by one as the gap between belonging to the class and facing consequences becomes undeniable — culminating in even the last holdouts choosing to conform once their old behavior no longer gets attention or amusement from peers.
points: Individualized interventions for multiple disruptive students (talking-tos, behavior contracts, personalized rewards) tend to worsen the problem by cementing a "difficult" label.
A class with several chronically disrespectful students is reframed as a classroom management problem, not an individual-student problem.
The fix requires starting over with sharply defined, non-negotiable boundaries applied to all students equally, taught and modeled thoroughly.
Change happens gradually and in order: well-behaved students respond first, then difficult students join one by one as peer support for misbehavior dries up.
quotes: One or two disrespectful students are hard enough. How do you handle a half dozen who are determined to make your life miserable?
You see, one of the most common mistakes teachers make is trying to handle difficult students as distinct entities, separate from the class as a whole.
But these individualized methods only make matters worse—because they encourage misbehavior.
The truth is, when you have several or more students who consistently disrupt learning and behave disrespectfully, it’s a sign you’ve lost control of your class—or never had it to begin with.
It’s a classroom management problem, not an individual student problem.
Your most well-behaved students will respond first. You’ll notice them smiling more and making eye contact with you.
You’ve made the gap between the experience of being part of the class, and the experience of being held accountable, so wide that no student can resist.
